newsitem.title: USA: U.S. balanced budget talks to continue Saturday.
newsitem.headline: U.S. balanced budget talks to continue Saturday.

text.p: Congressional Republicans Friday agreed to White House demands to restore disability aid to legal immigrants affected by a sweeping welfare law, as the two sides moved closer to a balanced budget deal.

Aides said administration officials and Republican leaders would resume talks Saturday in an effort to wrap up outstanding spending and tax issues. Republicans have set an Aug. 1 deadline for passing final budget bills.
"The plan is to finish the entire package," said Susan Irby, spokeswoman for Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott.

Lott, House Speaker Newt Gingrich and top administration officials were closeted in a Capitol hideaway most of Friday discussing possible compromises on spending legislation and a companion bill cutting taxes by $85 billion over five years.
Earlier Friday, Senate Budget Committee Chairman Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, said only a handful of spending items remained open.
Items under discussion included a new children's health programme, labour protections for welfare recipients in workfare programmes and major changes in Medicare, aides said.
They cautioned no decisions, including the welfare immigrant fix, were final until the whole deal was done.
"No agreement to cut spending will go into effect until the president agrees to cut taxes," said Ari Fleischer, House Ways and Means Committee spokesman.

A landmark welfare law signed last year will end most federal benefits to legal immigrants this fall. Clinton has been pushing to partially restore such aid, but Republicans had taken a hard line in the current budget talks.

Congressional aides said Republican leaders and the White House reached a deal Friday to continue Supplemental Security Income (SSI) disability benefits to all legal immigrants on the rolls as of Aug. 22, 1996, when the welfare bill was signed. That would affect about 500,000 immigrants.
In addition, immigrants in the country on that date who became disabled in the future would be eligible for aid. An estimated 150,000 immigrants would be covered.

The agreement, which had been part of the Senate budget bill, goes beyond original White House demands. The budget pact does not restore Food Stamps, however. About a million immigrants will lose nutrition aid this fall.
Republicans also dropped a plan, opposed by the White House, that would have let states reduce special supplemental payments to elderly individuals receiving SSI.

They agreed to an administration demand to continue Medicaid to tens of thousands of children who will lose SSI under the welfare law. The law end payments to children suffering from behaviourial rather than physical ailments.
"I think we're going to get this agreement," Clinton told an education group earlier Friday, after discussing the negotiations with top aides.
But tough issues remain.

Republicans have agreed to provide at least $16 billion for a new initiative to cover many of the nation's 10 million uninsured children. The White House wants an additional $8 billion, which was passed by the Senate as part of a 20-cents-per-pack increase in the cigarette tax.

Among major disagreements on the tax bill, the White House opposes a Republican tax plan indexing capital gains for inflation. Administration officials are also pushing to extend a $500-per-child tax credit to low-income workers.
The tax bill would reduce revenues by $85 billion over five years. The spending measure includes $115 billion in Medicare reductions and about $15 billion in Medicaid cuts.
As Republicans sped up the talks, some Democrats tried to apply the brakes warning Clinton not to rush into a deal.

Led by New York Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, Democrats on the influential Senate Finance Committee asked Clinton to defer final action until the fall if necessary in order to work out legislation that met party priorities.

They predicted the federal budget deficit could shrink to about $30 billion at the close of fiscal 1997, which ends Sept. 30. If current trends continued, the budget could be in balance next year without new action by Congress.
